title: Replication lag just spiked — what breaks, and how do you defend against it?
summary: Tests whether you can name concrete failure symptoms of replication lag and a real mitigation, not just repeat that replicas can lag.

slides.markdown:
"Replicas can be stale" is the vague, ungraded version of this answer. The interviewer wants the concrete version: which symptom shows up first, where it surfaces, and what you'd actually build to catch it before users complain.

This topic gives you that path — from the abstract fact that replication has lag, to a specific number, a specific user-visible failure, and a specific mitigation you can defend.

Ask where reads actually go: if every read hits the primary, replication lag is invisible to users no matter how large it gets — it only matters once **reads are routed to replicas** for scale. That single question reframes the whole answer.

Also ask whether this is a single-region setup with millisecond replication, or cross-region with tens or hundreds of milliseconds baseline lag — the failure mode and the fix both change with that number.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: symptom, then mitigation
slides.markdown:
Structure the answer as **symptom → mitigation**, not "lag exists." Symptom: a user's own write disappears on refresh, or two users see contradictory states of the same object. Mitigation: read-after-write routing to the primary for a short window, lag monitoring with an alert threshold, and replica health checks that pull a lagging node out of rotation.

Naming the mitigation before being asked is the difference between describing a problem and designing a system.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a comment disappears on refresh
slides.markdown:
![Replication lag makes a fresh write vanish](assets/replication-lag-sequence.svg)

A user posts a comment, the write lands on the primary, and their very next request — a page refresh — gets routed by the load balancer to a replica that hasn't caught up yet. The comment they just wrote is simply absent from the response.

This is the single most common way replication lag becomes a support ticket: not "data is eventually consistent" in the abstract, but "my own action just got undone," which reads as a bug even when the system is working exactly as designed.

assets.alt: Replication lag makes a fresh write vanish

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: lag jumping from 50ms to 8 seconds
slides.markdown:
A concrete worked number: replication lag normally sits around 50ms, then a bulk write job (a nightly import, a backfill migration) saturates the primary's write throughput and the replication stream falls behind — lag jumps to 8 seconds.

```
lag_ms = replica.applied_offset_lag(primary.wal_position)
# normal:   lag_ms ≈ 50
# incident: lag_ms ≈ 8000   during the bulk job window
```

At 50ms, almost no read-after-write case notices. At 8 seconds, any user who acts and then reads within that window — which is most users — sees stale or missing data. The failure isn't replication itself; it's the bulk job's write volume overwhelming the replication pipeline's normal capacity.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a lag-monitoring alert before users complain
slides.markdown:
Naming the proactive piece matters as much as the reactive fix: an alert fires the moment replication lag on any replica crosses a stated threshold — say, 2 seconds — well before enough users hit the read-after-write window to start filing tickets.

The threshold itself should be a product decision, not an arbitrary engineering number: pick it based on how long after writing a typical user is likely to read their own data again, then alert comfortably below that.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
**Routing more reads to the primary to dodge lag protects correctness but removes the scaling benefit replicas exist for.** Replicas exist specifically to take read load off the primary — sending reads back to it defeats that purpose for the traffic you route back.

| Choice | You pay in | You gain |
|---|---|---|
| Route all reads to primary | Primary becomes the bottleneck again | Zero staleness |
| Route reads to replicas | Replicas can serve stale data during lag spikes | Real horizontal read scaling |
| Route only the writer's own reads to primary | A short window of extra primary load, per writer | Read-your-writes without losing general scaling |

The third row is usually the answer worth defending — it targets the fix at exactly the users who'd notice.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how would you even detect lag has grown?
slides.markdown:
Name the concrete signal: every replica can report how far behind the primary's write position it is — a log sequence number or WAL offset gap, converted to a time estimate. Emit that as a metric per replica, graph it, and alert on it crossing a threshold.

Don't rely on user complaints as your detection mechanism — by the time someone reports stale data, the lag has likely been elevated for a while. A dashboard showing lag per replica, refreshed every few seconds, is the concrete artifact to name here.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: fix the symptom or the root cause?
slides.markdown:
If the bulk write job is the actual cause, routing reads around lag treats the symptom, not the disease — the right long-term fix is throttling or rescheduling the bulk job (running it at low-traffic hours, rate-limiting its write rate, or running it against a dedicated replica that read traffic never touches).

Say both: a short-term mitigation to stop the bleeding now, and a root-cause fix so the same incident doesn't recur next time the job runs.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming lag is always milliseconds
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Replication lag is a few milliseconds, so it's not worth designing around."

**Why it's wrong:** lag is only milliseconds under normal load. A bulk job, a network blip, or a replica falling behind on disk I/O can push it to seconds and, in genuinely bad cases, minutes — and that's exactly when the largest number of users are reading data they (or someone else) just wrote.

**Correct model:** budget for a multi-second lag spike as a normal operating condition, not an outage, and design the read path (monitoring, routing, alerting) around that assumption from the start.

"Replication lag isn't abstract — it shows up as a user's own write vanishing on refresh, or two readers seeing contradictory state. I'd name the concrete symptom, then the mitigation: read-after-write routing for the writer's own reads, a lag-monitoring alert well below the threshold where users would notice, and health checks that pull a badly lagging replica out of rotation. I'd also chase the root cause — often a bulk job saturating the replication stream — rather than only routing around the symptom."

See [synchronous-vs-asynchronous-replication](synchronous-vs-asynchronous-replication) for why this lag exists in the first place.
